[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Across word boundaries, assimilation of identical moving consonants is best when it yields five or more consecutive moving segments; such sequences are generally avoided in five-letter words.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Silencing is not allowed in qurādd or lahāmm because it would impose a plural pattern unlike their singulars; poems by an unnamed poet and Ghaylān b. Ḥurayth support concealment.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | A reading with kasra in ʿayn of niʿimmā follows the dialect that vocalizes ʿayn; Abū al-Khaṭṭāb identifies it as Hudhayl, and Ṭarafa’s verse supports the form. | mentions 4:58
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل مكة | reports | For falā tatanājaw, the first tāʾ may be quiescent after the long vowel or concealed with moving weight; Meccans reportedly do not fully articulate both tāʾs. | mentions 58:9
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In thawb Bakr, clear articulation is better than after a long vowel because the preceding vowel is not part of the same word; concealment or silence remains possible with long-vowel letters.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The yāʾ in diminutive ṣuwaym is not moved, resembling alif in plural patterns; this permits concealment or, with its length, silence.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A final long wāw or yāʾ followed by the same initial sound in the next word is not assimilated, as in dalw Wāqid and ẓaby Yāsir.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With final long yāʾ or wāw followed by the same sound, speakers may conceal or articulate across the boundary but cannot silence it because that removes length; rhyme evidence confirms this.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A wāw after ḍamma or yāʾ after kasra is not assimilated across a word boundary; speakers preserve the long vowel and the form's weight.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In imperatives such as ikhshi Yāsiran and ikhshū Wāqidan, assimilation occurs because these yāʾs and wāws are not long vowels in this use.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Two hamzas are not assimilated because speakers must preserve distinct pronunciation; Ibn Abī Isḥāq and his associates used assimilation, which Sībawayh calls poor but permissible for them.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poetic meter supports the preference: five moving consonants do not occur consecutively in verse, though clear pronunciation remains good Hijazi Arabic.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r20] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In iftaʿala forms such as iqtatalū and yaqtatilūn, speakers may show or conceal the matching tāʾs; unlike fixed gemination in iḥmarra, the infix tāʾ need not be followed by its matching radical.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r21] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعض العرب | reports | Some Arabs fully assimilate the tāʾs in a single word, quiescing the first; others transfer its movement to the prior consonant, with both forms possible in these flexible sequences.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r22] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan’s reading illā man khaṭifa al-khaṭfata supports the account of assimilation and alternative vocalizations of the preceding consonant. | mentions 37:10
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r23] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل وهارون | reports | Al-Khalīl and Hārūn report speakers saying murdifīn for murta difīn; this is a Meccan reading, with muqtalīn a rarer parallel and radif for irtadaf in another dialect.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r24] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The alif in ألْحمر is retained after moving lām because it resembles hamzat qaṭʿ: it opens initially and remains under interrogation; similar strengthening occurs in other phrases.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r25] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Assimilation in iqtatalū is as good as across-word jaʿal laka, though adjacency also makes it resemble the fixed gemination of iḥmarra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r26] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | There is no concealment in اردد because the consonant is between two quiescent letters; رد داود behaves like اسم موسى, with assimilation only when the preceding segment is moving.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Unlike assimilation within a word, separate words can be pronounced distinctly because the second word need not begin with the matching consonant.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Assimilation is also good when another moving matching consonant precedes the pair and a quiescent consonant follows, as in yad Dāwūd.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The more consecutive movements there are, the better assimilation becomes, though distinct pronunciation remains permissible.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A long vowel before matching moving consonants counts like a moving segment, so assimilation is good in examples such as inna al-māla laka.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A long vowel acts like a moving segment and supplies the raddif required when a moving segment is deleted in rhyme; the yāʾ in the cited poetry supplies the raddif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If a quiescent consonant precedes the first matching moving consonant, it cannot be silenced; speakers may hide it with moving weight because boundary assimilation does not change word structure.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالإدغامفيالحرفيناللذينتضعلسانكلهماموضعاواحدالا#807/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Examples such as ibn Nūḥ and ism Mūsā retain their forms; assimilation shifting a consonant inside one word can delete its alif, as in رد and قل, while cross-word assimilation would alter the word's structure.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hamza following a quiescent consonant has several pausal realizations, including forms with a hinted or applied case vowel.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For softened hamza after ḍamma or kasra, the replacement is wāw or yāʾ respectively, without ishām, as in akmū and ahnā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When hamza after a quiescent consonant is softened, it must be deleted; the consonant that receives its movement then follows ordinary pausal rules for nonweak consonants.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Many Arabs, especially Tamīm and Asad, vocalize the consonant before hamza to clarify hamza, which is especially faint at pause.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ناس من بني تميم | reports | Some Banū Tamīm say al-radiʾ rather than add ḍamma after kasra, rejecting a faʿl sequence, and regularize accusative and al-baṭʾ similarly.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · من العرب | reports | Some speakers replace final hamza with wāw in the nominative, yāʾ in the genitive, and alif in the accusative while keeping the preceding consonant quiescent.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Speakers who avoid the preceding-vowel strategy should consistently retain the corresponding wāw or yāʾ alternatives.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the consonant before hamza already has a vowel, hamza takes the usual pausal options; the same applies when a quiescent preceding consonant is first moved.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Speakers avoid doubling final hamza, so it otherwise behaves like a nonweak consonant except in replacement and gemination.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · من العرب | reports | Some speakers replace final hamza in al-kalʾ with wāw, yāʾ, or alif according to case, as in the variants of al-wathʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابالوقففيالهمز)#736/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | Hijazi speakers who do not realize hamza pronounce a quiescent hamza after fatḥa as alif in every case; no ishām applies because it is like the dual alif.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتقلبفيهالياءواوا)#787/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the quadriliteral pattern, yāʾ can become wāw in the verb when the form is long and its yāʾ is not inherently mobile; Sibawayh cites taʿayyaṭat and the rajaz form ʿawṭaṭ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Final weak radicals are most defective, medial ones stronger, and initial ones strongest, because endings bear case, nunation, pronoun

attachment, and dual formation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In some plurals yāʾ is preferred, as in thady and ʿaṣī; some speakers analogize these forms to ʿatū, while the yāʾ plural remains common.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A wāw preceded by kasra always turns into yāʾ, as in ghāzin and related forms; Sibawayh cites ʿAbd Yaghūth's verse as evidence for the alternation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After an added alif, a final weak radical is hamzated, as in qaḍāʾ and namāʾ, because it is more defective after fatḥa than after ḍamma or kasra.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In dialectal reduced forms such as ghazi and shaqi, yāʾ remains because the form was already yāʾ after an original vowelled radical; this differs from a form like raḍiyū with a still radical.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With raḍiyū, the radical stays still like ghazi; if it were kasra-vowelled, two sukūns would meet. Sarūw likewise varies by whether its vowel is retained.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms from hamzated roots show yāʾ conversion for movement: jīʾ becomes jī when lightened, and quadriliteral jūyi likewise becomes jī, like muwayqin and luwayya; this is unlike ghazā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The imperfect vowel of a verb with final wāw or yāʾ is controlled by the following weak radical: wāw verbs use yafʿulu and yāʾ verbs use yafʿilu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The faʿula pattern occurs with wāw, as sarā/yasrū, but not yāʾ: Arabs avoid transferring the lighter yāʾ to the heavier wāw throughout a verb's inflection.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A final wāw after ḍamma is weak and resists ḍamma, while fatḥa is tolerated as lighter; Sibawayh illustrates with yaghzūka and anṣaba forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A final yāʾ after kasra resists genitive inflection, as final wāw after ḍamma does; accusative fatḥa remains because it is lighter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Final wāw and yāʾ after fatḥa become alif in forms such as ramā/yarmā and ghazā/yaghzā; the weak radical's vowel is carried by what follows.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Before consonantal suffixes, final weak radicals retain their original wāw or yāʾ because the lām is not mobile; alif conversion occurs only when it is underlyingly vowelled.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A declensional final wāw after ḍamma changes to yāʾ and the preceding vowel becomes kasra, as in dalw/adlin, to accommodate case and suffixes; non-final wāw can remain.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماكانتالياءوالواوفيلامات)#789/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When a consonant precedes weak wāw or yāʾ, the pair behaves like sound radicals; examples include ẓaby and dalw, though speakers also analogize some forms to inflected nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمالايردمنهذهالأحرفالثلاثةلتحركمابعدهاوسأخبركلم#728/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In jussive singular weak verbs such as lam yakhaf, lam yabiʿ, and lam yaqul, the weak letter stays deleted; its deletion is not reversed when the following context no longer requires it.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمالايردمنهذهالأحرفالثلاثةلتحركمابعدهاوسأخبركلم#728/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In dual jussives such as lam yakhāfā, lam yaqūlā, and lam yabīʿā, the long vowels are fixed dual markers; only the nūn is deleted for jussive mood.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For wāw-medial faʿl nouns, the small-count plural is usually afʿāl, avoiding the heavy ḍamma in afʿul.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The plurals arwāḥ and riyāḥ, like abār and biʾār, retain the patterns used for wāw-medial nouns rather than following the yāʾ class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Other wāw-medial faʿl nouns take afʿāl in small counts and fiʿlān in larger counts; this distinguishes them from the yāʾ class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For feminine weak-medial nouns such as ʿaybah, ḍayʿah, and rawḍah, larger plurals follow sound-noun patterns; small counts can add -āt without moving the medial weak letter.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some wāw-medial feminine nouns instead use fuʿul broken plurals, as nūbah/nuwab, jawbah/juwab, dawlah/duwal, and qaryah/qurā.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The yāʾ-medial forms ḍayʿah/ḍayʿ and khaymah/khiyam use fuʿul as a non-regular pattern, by analogy with sound nouns.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A feminine pattern with a weak second radical can form small counts with -āt without changing that radical; without -āt it may take a broken plural such as duwal or suq.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Another feminine weak pattern permits both sound plurals in -āt and broken plurals: qīmah/qiyam, rībah/ribāt and rib, and dīmah/dīm.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Feminine faʿlah nouns such as nāqah commonly form plurals on fiʿāl, though fuʿul also occurs; their small-count plurals take -āt.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some feminine weak forms have exceptional plurals such as ʾaynūq and qiyam; the poet's tārāt/tīr witnesses a yāʾ-related broken plural.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Larger counts of these wāw nouns commonly take fiʿāl; fiʿlān also occurs, while some forms remain limited to afʿāl.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A few forms preserve the original afʿul pattern despite its rarity; qaws/aqwus is given, alongside the rajaz witness athwāb.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For yāʾ-medial faʿl nouns, afʿāl is the small-count pattern, with occasional afʿul; larger counts favor fuʿūl, lighter than the wāw pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Hollow nouns such as qāʿ, tāj, and jār take afʿāl for small counts and fiʿlān for larger counts; fiʿāl is infrequent and fuʿūl is avoided.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yūnus says feminine hollow faʿl nouns such as dār, sāq, and nār form small-count plurals on afʿul.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh questions a feminine-gender explanation for afʿul, since feminine nouns such as raḥā, qafā, qadam, and ghanam also show other patterns.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Larger-count plurals of dār and sāq include fuʿul, with variants such as dīrān and diyār; nīb for the she-camel avoids the disliked yāʾ-and-ḍamma sequence.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابنظيرماذكرنامنبناتالياءوالواوالتيالياءاتوالواوات#656/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Nouns on fīl take afʿāl for small counts and fuʿūl for larger counts; some also use plural forms in -ah, while afʿāl may be the only attested pattern.
